title: KV cache
simple: A KV cache stores attention keys and values from previous tokens so decoding need not recompute them for each new token. Its memory grows with workload and model architecture.
analogy: Keep earlier calculations on a scratchpad instead of recalculating every line. More simultaneous students and longer worksheets need more scratch space.
engineering: A simplified dense cache byte count is 2 × layers × KV heads × head dimension × tokens × batch × bytes per element. The factor two covers keys and values.
Grouped-query and multi-query attention reduce KV heads. Runtime layouts, paging, quantization, tensor parallelism and other memory allocations affect actual GPU use.
example: For 32 layers, 32 KV heads, head dimension 128, 4,096 tokens, batch 1 and 2-byte elements, cache size is 2,147,483,648 bytes = 2 GiB. Eight KV heads under the same assumptions use 0.5 GiB.
misconception: KV memory is not a universal 0.5 MB per token, and weight size alone cannot establish GPU fit.

exercise.prompt: Use the GPU calculator to change KV heads from 32 to 8 and batch from 1 to 4.
exercise.solution: Heads divided by four reduce the simplified cache fourfold; batch multiplied by four restores the original cache total. Add weights and measured runtime overhead before judging capacity.

interview.question: How would you estimate whether a model fits a GPU?
interview.answer: Estimate weight bytes, architecture-specific KV cache at target context and concurrency, and runtime overhead. Leave headroom, then measure peak memory and throughput on the actual implementation.
interview.followUp: How do paged caches and batching change fragmentation and throughput?
interview.followUpAnswer: Paged caches can reduce allocation waste and support flexible scheduling; batching can improve utilization while increasing active cache demand and waiting time. Measure peak memory, fragmentation, throughput and time-to-first/token latency at realistic sequence lengths and concurrency.

title: Quantization
simple: Quantization represents weights or activations using lower-precision formats. It can save memory and change speed, with quality and hardware-dependent trade-offs.
analogy: A photograph can be stored with fewer color levels. The file becomes smaller, but details may change and the reader must support the format.
engineering: Distinguish weight-only, activation and KV-cache quantization. Scale factors, group metadata and runtime buffers add overhead beyond the nominal bit count.
Benchmark quality, latency and hardware kernel support. Reduced weight size does not guarantee proportional speedup or more users.
example: Seven billion parameters require about 14 GB at 16 bits or 3.5 GB at 4 bits before scales, metadata and runtime allocations. These are decimal GB, not total GPU memory.
misconception: Four-bit weights do not guarantee a fourfold throughput or concurrency increase.

exercise.prompt: Use the GPU calculator to compare 16-bit and 4-bit weights while keeping a long-context cache fixed.
exercise.solution: Only the modeled weight allocation shrinks. KV state and overhead remain unless independently changed; cache-heavy workloads may still exceed capacity.

interview.question: When would you quantize a model?
interview.answer: When measured memory or serving constraints justify it and the quality drop is acceptable on representative tasks. Check hardware support, calibration data, total memory and latency rather than relying on nominal bits alone.
interview.followUp: How would outlier values or a domain shift affect a quantized model?
interview.followUpAnswer: Lower precision can distort sensitive or outlier values, and calibration data may fail to represent the target workload. Compare representative slices and regression cases with the baseline. Hardware kernels, scales and metadata affect both memory and speed, so benchmark the actual serving stack.

title: Fine-tuning and LoRA
simple: Fine-tuning changes model parameters for a task. LoRA trains smaller low-rank updates while keeping selected base weights frozen. It is different from adding facts through retrieval.
analogy: Instead of rewriting every page of a textbook, you attach a compact set of adjustments to how a student solves a task. The adjustments still need good examples and testing.
engineering: For a matrix with input width d_in and output width d_out, a rank-r LoRA pair has r(d_in + d_out) parameters. Sum over adapted matrices.

Separate train, validation and test data; inspect leakage and licensing. Training memory also includes base weights, activations, optimizer state and other buffers. Evaluate regressions and deployment compatibility.
example: For a 4,096 × 4,096 matrix at rank 8, LoRA adds 8 × 8,192 = 65,536 parameters versus 16,777,216 full-matrix parameters, about 0.391%. This is one matrix, not a whole-model training-memory estimate.
misconception: A small adapter is not the total training memory, and fine-tuning is not a reliable substitute for fresh authorized knowledge.

exercise.prompt: Compare RAG, prompt examples and LoRA for changing policy facts versus enforcing a repeated output style.
exercise.solution: Use retrieval for changing source-grounded facts. Start with prompts/examples for style and evaluate fine-tuning when enough representative data and a persistent measured gap justify it. Keep factual validation after adaptation.

interview.question: When would you use LoRA instead of RAG?
interview.answer: They solve different problems and can coexist. LoRA can adapt behavior or task patterns; RAG supplies updateable, attributable evidence. Choose from measured failure modes, data quality, operating constraints and held-out evaluations.
interview.followUp: How would you detect memorization, leakage or a regression after adapter training?
interview.followUpAnswer: Audit train/validation/test separation and near-duplicates, evaluate held-out and adversarial cases and compare the base model plus prompt/RAG baselines. Track memorized sensitive strings, domain and general-task regressions and adaptation data provenance. Keep a reproducible adapter version and rollback path.

stages.detail: Compare against prompts and retrieval baselines.
